sections.subject: ANTH
sections.title: BIOLOGICAL ANTHROPOLOGY: Exploring Diversity In Healthcare
sections.note: This course explores the intersection of human diversity and healthcare, focusing on how biological, social, and cultural differences influence health outcomes. Through a problem-based learning approach, students investigate contemporary issues related to race, gender, and other social categories, with an emphasis on understanding when and how diversity should be integrated into healthcare delivery and policy. Students will critically analyze how healthcare systems either accommodate or marginalize diverse populations and will develop evidence-based strategies to promote inclusive, equitable care.

sections.note: This course runs every Saturday and Sunday in March. You will be working outdoors. We recommend dressing in layers, in clothes that can get dirty. sections.title: TOPICS IN CANADIAN STUDIES: How to Change the World: Canadian Grassroots Organizations
sections.note: Grassroots community organizations are at the heart of much social, environmental and economic change in Canada. They have historically been the “small groups of committed citizens” that “change the world” for the better. This course explores the history, achievements and possibilities inherent in grassroots organizations in Canada, using provocative examples from across the country but with a focus on British Columbia movements. The course will also include a community-engaged component, offering opportunity for students to engage with a local community organization, pairing their class learning on the theory, practice and history of grassroots social and environmental justice movements with on-the-ground experience.

sections.subject: ES
sections.title: ADV TPC:POLITICAL ECOLOGY: Indigenous Environmental Justice Movements
sections.note: Topic description: While environmental justice gained recognition as a movement in the 1980’s, Indigenous communities have organized to respond to the harmful impacts of pollution, resource extraction, industrial development, and other forms of environmental injustice for centuries. This course uses an interdisciplinary approach to examine global processes that have contributed to environmental justice issues, as well as unpack some of the common assumptions underlying ideas about the environment, how we relate to it, and who is affected by changes in ideological and management paradigms.

sections.subject: ES
sections.title: ADV TPC:POLITICAL ECOLOGY: Queer and Trans Ecologies
sections.note: Topic description: This class brings queer and trans theories into conversation with environmental studies to examine how heteropatriarchal and cisnormativity shape environmental thought and efforts, while creating space to explore the expansive possibilities within queer and trans ecologies.

sections.subject: ES
sections.title: ADV TPC:ECOLOGICAL RESTORATN: Canadian Mammal Conservation Ecology
sections.note: Topic description: this seminar course explores the major pressing topics in Canadian mammal conservation and the ecological theories around species declines and recoveries. Students will get exposed to a comprehensive survey of Canadian mammal species, their conservation status, and the ecological problems facing species at risk. Through joint reading, discussion, and exploration of primary literature, students will develop a fulsome understanding of why Canadian mammal species are in decline and how conservation efforts are succeeding or failing to stem those declines.

sections.subject: ES
sections.title: ADV TPC:ECOLOGICAL RESTORATN: Forest Environments
sections.note: Topic description: In this course we will review key concepts and recent research focused on forested ecosystems. Topics explored in lecture and seminar sessions will include forest ecosystem services, forest composition and biodiversity, forest livelihoods, forest governance, and alternative forest economies. Several class sessions will be held outside and in a computer lab to explore field and GIS methods to characterize forest structure and composition.

sections.subject: PSYC
sections.title: SPECIAL TOPICS IN PSYC: Family Psychology
sections.note: Prerequisites: PSYC 201 and PSYC 243. This course examines the psychological processes that shape family relationships across the lifespan. We will explore how families form, function, and change over time, with a focus on core dynamics such as marriage and divorce, parent-child and sibling relationships, communication, conflict, and caregiving. The course also considers how broader social, cultural, and historical contexts influence family life. Drawing on research in family and relationship science, the course emphasizes how psychological principles and empirical evidence can be applied to better understand real-world family relationships and to inform more effective ways of navigating them.

sections.subject: PSYC
sections.title: TPCS: ADV COGNITIVE PSYCHOLOGY: The Dynamics of Cognitive Control in Aging
sections.note: Description: In this class, we will learn all about age-related changes in cognitive control, and how those changes impact performance on memory and other cognitive tasks.

sections.subject: PSYC
sections.title: TPC:ADV COGNITIVE NEUROSCIENCE: Computational Beauty of Mind
sections.note: Description: This is an advanced undergraduate seminar on computational modeling of cognition. We will work with a variety of approaches to cognitive modeling and learn how they have been used to understand different mental processes. As an upper-level seminar, students will be expected to take an active role in the course and engage with the material.

sections.subject: PSYC
sections.title: SPECIAL TOPICS CLINICAL PSYC: Climate Anxiety and Grief
sections.note: Description: This course explores recent epidemiological data linking climate anxiety and grief to adverse mental health outcomes across the globe. We survey research from multiple academic disciplines demonstrating the adverse impacts of climate anxiety/grief on human emotions, cognitions, behaviours and systems. We connect experientially with our own climate distress and practice interventions designed to restore our courage and our sense of purpose for climate engagement.

sections.subject: PSYC
sections.title: ADV SPCL TPCS:PSYC: Psychology for Instruction
sections.note: Description: Psychological science has much to contribute to enhancing teaching and learning across a range of educational contexts. Drawing on contemporary research, this course will explore evidenced-based principles from psychology that inform the design of effective and responsive learning environments. The course will be of interest to students who are interested in (a) applying psychological science to instructional design or assessment, (b) developing instructional tools and interventions, (c ) pursuing careers related to education or instructional design, or (d) contributing to research in the psychology of education. This is a good course for future teaching assistants.

sections.subject: PSYC
sections.title: ADV SPCL TPCS:PSYC: Health Across the Lifespan
sections.note: Prerequisites: PSYC 300A and two of: PSYC 335, 336, 339, 391. Description: Taking a life course perspective, this seminar examines how health develops and changes across the lifespan, from childhood through older adulthood. Students will (a) explore psychological and behavioral determinants of health within social and contextual environments, including family relationships, schools, neighborhoods, and broader sociocultural contexts; (b) examine how these multilevel processes shape patterns of health, inequality, and resilience over time; and (c) engage with major psychological theories and research methods, as well as emerging social and technological contexts, to critically evaluate both academic research and popular health information.

sections.subject: PSYC
sections.title: TOPICS IN COMMUNITY ENGAGEMENT: Working in the Community
sections.note: Prerequisites: 4th year standing; PSYC 300A and one of PSYC 332, PSYC 336, PSYC 345A, PSYC 366, PSYC 375, PSYC 385, PSYC 386, PSYC 387. This is the first half of a course that runs Sep-Apr. You must register in the same section in Second Term (Jan-Apr) to complete your registration. For example, register in PHIL100 A01 in First Term and PHIL100 A01 in Second Term. Off-campus component: This course includes a placement consisting of a minimum of 40 hours of unpaid work with a community organization or on a community project. Placement schedules are co-created between students and community, with support from instructor. While this does not imply more overall time dedication to this course, students should consider if their schedule can accommodate community experience. Description: In this community-engaged learning course, students will engage with a community-serving organization, a school, and/or a local community to address research questions and/or implement and evaluate programs that promote the well-being of children, youth, young adults, seniors and/or their family from diverse social, economic, and cultural backgrounds, across developmental transitions, and in evolving societal circumstances. As a professional development course, students will also learn about theories and methods related to community-engaged research, knowledge mobilization, and program evaluation.

sections.subject: PSYC
sections.title: TOPICS IN COMMUNITY ENGAGEMENT: Reducing Stereotyping, Prejudice, and Discrimination
sections.note: Prerequisites: PSYC300A and PSYC387. Description: This course is an in-depth examination of theoretical, empirical, and applied approaches to reducing stereotyping, prejudice, and discrimination from a social psychological perspective. Considers bottom-up and top-down approaches to improving intergroup relations. This course has a significant community engagement component and considers link to employable skills. This course also includes an event on April 9th at 4:30-7:20pm that all registered students are required to attend. Community-engaged learning component: This course includes a placement consistent of a minimum of 20 hours of in person volunteering with a community organization. Reciprocity is a very important value in a community-engaged learning course. Therefore, your course work may involve work that will be shared with the community partner, and the community partner may use this for their purposes. This course will involve a substantial amount of collaboration, teamwork, in-depth self-reflection and introspection, interactive activities, as well as consistent in person attendance for volunteer shifts and for class time. This course involves placing a lot of trust in students working with vulnerable populations, therefore being present is crucial. International students interested in this community-engaged learning course should contact the International Centre for Students (ICS) to discuss potential work authorization requirements for the experiential learning component of this course.
